idiom_name: two linked subclasses, one per parent hierarchy, created and wired by a factory
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define one end per parent hierarchy, each deriving from its parent and answering that parent's protocol; give every end one field holding its partner plus one forwarding method per message that must cross the link; create both ends together in a factory, link them in both directions before either is published, and return the end the caller asked for; keep the pair inside one package or module so the crossing calls need no public access. Decide identity (which end is canonical for equality, locking and logging) and lifetime (which direction may be weak or cleared on teardown) explicitly, and treat 'both links set' as a class invariant no client can break.
pitfalls: Publishing one end before the link exists: clients then observe a null or stale twin reference.
Letting both ends own each other strongly in a runtime that does not collect cycles: neither end is ever released.
Forgetting that state inherited from a shared base class is duplicated per end, so a 'shared' field silently exists twice.

Wrong move: hand-crafting a twin pair in a language that can supply the second parent natively - default methods (Java 8+), interface delegation (Kotlin), traits (Scala), mixins (Python, Ruby) - -> the pair duplicates glue the language could provide and every future subclass must keep both ends and all forwarding methods in step -> instead: verify the second parent carries code and state that no interface, mixin or delegation clause can bring in, and twin only the genuine implementation-inheritance case.

Wrong move: letting a platform callback on one end re-enter the other end while it is mid-update, e.g. a click on the item end toggling state while the run loop is between draw and move -> interleaved access to state owned by the other end loses updates and tears frames -> instead: guard crossing calls with an explicit volatile suspended/active flag as in the paper's suspend/resume, or fix a lock ordering, and document which end may call the other during a transition.

Wrong move: leaving equals, hashCode and lock choice at their defaults on both ends -> two clients holding opposite ends of one logical entity observe different identities, and synchronizing on one end fails to exclude a writer holding the other -> instead: nominate one end as canonical for identity and locking, delegate the other end's equals/hashCode to it, and record the rule where both ends are visible.
